look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST · UNARMED scrambling or climbing nightshade with often LOBED ovate leaves, PURPLE corolla lobes strongly REFLEXED backward, a close-packed yellow ANTHER CONE, and clusters of shiny RED berries. Flower clusters commonly much branched with 7–40 flowers. Leaf basal lobes, anther arrangement and cluster branching are better together than berry color alone. RARE WHITE-flowered bittersweet exists. Texas nightshade (S. triquetrum) can also scramble and make red fruit, but generally has smaller white flowers, more individually distinct yellow anthers, sharply triangular/hastate leaves and 3–6-flowered clusters. Do NOT eat berries; introduced comparison, not a locally certified native.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew accepts the species but treats it as native to Eurasia/North Africa, not Texas.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Included for visual learning; native metrics excluded unless later exact-county review supports inclusion.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Solanaceae/Solanum: alternate leaves, 5-parted rotate/stellate corollas, poricidal anthers, and berry fruits.
best_field_traits: UNARMED woody or herbaceous SCRAMBLING vine-like perennial (not a true tendril vine); older stems can persist.
ALTERNATE petiolate leaves usually ovate/heart-shaped, often with one or two pointed SIDE LOBES near base; some leaves entirely unlobed.
5-part DEEPLY REFLEXED purple/violet petals (rare WHITE); shiny GREEN/WHITE markings near petal bases may be visible in larger macros, not reliably visible in existing photo.
Yellow anthers 4.5–6 mm (Flora of North America), held CONNIVENT/clustered into a compact cone; never call them 'fused' solely from ordinary photos.
Many-branched, often 7–40-flowered clusters; pedicels insert into small sleeves on axis. Flowers roughly 1.5–2 cm wide.
Shiny red mature berries roughly 0.5–1.5 cm long and green/purplish five-lobed calyces at base, as visible in current exact-species fruit photograph.
FNA lists introduced-range occurrence widely in North America. Preserve this project's COMPARISON_NONNATIVE native-metrics exclusion.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: SOLANUM DULCAMARA vs TEXAS NIGHTSHADE: purple REFLEXED corolla and tightly CONNIVENT yellow anthers, many-branched 7–40-flower clusters, ovate to basally lobed leaves versus usually small WHITE flowers with more separate FREE anthers, 3–6-flowered clusters, sharply triangular/hastate leaves and more angular stems. Exceptions: white-flowered S. dulcamara; both make red fruit, both scramble.
morphology_keys.habit: Unarmed, sprawling/scrambling woody-based perennial, sometimes climbing through shrubs and fences; no prickles, tendrils, or adventitious adhesive pads required. Avoid calling it a twining vine without observing the mechanics.
morphology_keys.leaves: Simple alternate petiolate blades, ovate to cordate, sometimes entire but often with basal side lobes (especially leaf at ~38% x,37% y in Piermario Maculan's berry photograph). Do not claim every leaf is lobed.
morphology_keys.flower: Small five-lobed corolla typically PURPLE/violet, petals REFLEXED dramatically backward; rare WHITE plants occur. Yellow anthers equal and held CONNIVENT in a close cone, ~4.5–6 mm in FNA; bright green/pale shiny spots at corolla lobe bases. Present flower JPEG supports purple reflexed petals and anther cone, but does not support measured anther length or precise green-eye arrow.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Terminal/lateral extra-axillary MANY-BRANCHED 7–40-flowered cyme, pedicels in slight sleeves on axis; significantly more flowers than S. triquetrum's generally 3–6. Current flower photo shows only part of a cluster, not reliable to count to 40.
morphology_keys.fruit: Round-ellipsoid glossy RED ripe berries, ~0.5–1.5 cm long, with persistent green to dark-purplish small five-lobed calyx and individual pedicels. Existing original Maculan photo actually shows mature red berries and visible calyx, so fruit-photo target is MET. Berry color alone can't separate S. dulcamara from S. triquetrum.
morphology_keys.habitat: Many habitats, often somewhat moist disturbed places, hedgerows, thickets and streambanks. Eurasian origin / introduced comparison in this project; keep Texas/county nativity unchanged.
morphology_keys.management: Poisonous/nightshade risk: do NOT taste berries, use as food, or direct children to handle and eat them. Classify locally with multiple botanical characters before any weed-management intervention.

field_terms.reflexed: Petal lobe bent backward away from the face of the flower.
field_terms.connivent: Anthers closely pressed together into a cone (not necessarily fused). Compare separated/free anthers in S. triquetrum.
field_terms.pedicel: Individual flower or berry stalk. The more branched inflorescence has several pedicels on a shared axis.
field_terms.calyx: Green/purplish five-sepal structure AT THE BASE of berry; visible as dark five-pointed crowns against red fruit in photo 2.
field_terms.hastate: Triangular, arrowhead-like leaf with pointing basal lobes (often seen on Texas nightshade, sometimes occurs on S. dulcamara).
field_terms.corolla_eye: Shiny green/white spots at flower-lobe bases. Too small for reliable labeling in current full-size flower photo.

crew_field_sequence: 1 · Confirm unarmed sprawling/scrambling Solanum, not a prickly nightshade.
2 · Inspect multiple leaves for OVATE/heart-like outlines and possible basal lobes; don't identify from one lobe shape.
3 · Examine open flower: five mostly PURPLE lobes bent backward and a cone of closely grouped yellow anthers. Some flowers may be WHITE.
4 · Find and photograph the FULL branched inflorescence; S. dulcamara may bear 7–40 flowers vs S. triquetrum usually 3–6.
5 · Inspect fruit carefully: genuine bright RED ripe berries with dark-green/purplish calyx and pedicel (both visible in photo 2). RED berries alone are not the final ID.
6 · Compare S. triquetrum: sharply triangular/hastate variable leaves, strongly angled stem, usually WHITE smaller flower with more separately visible yellow anthers.
7 · If only ripe red fruit without flowers or leaf/branch arrangement, record 'red-berried Solanum—compare S. dulcamara / S. triquetrum' until diagnostic views are available.
8 · Never taste berries or rely on berry 'edibility' folklore for field ID.

field_matrix.flower: Usually PURPLE deeply reflexed; sometimes WHITE; 4.5–6 mm CONNIVENT yellow anthers forming tight cone
field_matrix.leaf: Ovate / heart-shaped; often with side lobes but variable
field_matrix.stems: Woody or herbaceous unarmed SCRAMBLING vine-like
field_matrix.fruit: Glossy RED when ripe; calyx and pedicel at berry base
field_matrix.quick_rule: Purple reflexed star + tight yellow cone + many branched flowers; color exception exists.

field_matrix.flower: Usually WHITE (can purple-tinge), smaller corolla; yellow anthers individually FREE, ~3.5–4 mm
field_matrix.fruit: Also shiny RED, so berry color alone fails
field_matrix.quick_rule: Sharp triangle leaves + few white flowers + free yellow anthers.

field_matrix.flower: Small WHITE stars, extremely short yellow anthers
field_matrix.stems: Upright/branching herb, not long scrambling woody vine
field_matrix.quick_rule: Smaller flower and black berries; different group, don't identify from leaf alone.

not_reliable_alone: Bright RED ripe berry: also present on Texas nightshade.
PURPLE vs WHITE corolla alone: white-flowered bittersweet nightshade occurs.
One single ovate or triangular leaf: variation overlaps.
Anther tips or flower green-eye spots inferred from blurry or low-resolution JPEG.
Assuming all North American records imply Texas or Hays County locality.

visual_comparison.title: Bittersweet nightshade — PURPLE swept-back petals, yellow ANTHER cone, RED berries
visual_comparison.subtitle: Two independently credited exact-species CC0 photographs teach flower/foliage and mature berries/calyces. A third panel is explicitly TEXAS NIGHTSHADE, a different species. 7 anatomically checked overlays on the two source photographs.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: PURPLE backwards petals + packed yellow anthers + branched many-flowered cyme + glossy RED berries. RARE WHITE-flowered S. dulcamara and red-fruited S. triquetrum demand multiple characters.

items.label: 1 — PURPLE reflexed corolla, CONNIVENT yellow anthers and basal-lobed leaf
items.image_role: Purple reflexed white-centered flowers, connivent yellow anther cone, green basal-lobed leaf
items.creator: Andrew Macumber
items.caption: This is bittersweet nightshade. Reflexed PURPLE corolla lobes reveal a yellow anther CONE, with the anthers held close together (connivent), not necessarily genetically fused. A green leaf behind the flower has basal side lobes. Photograph Andrew Macumber / Wikimedia Commons (CC0).
items.why_it_matters: Look first for the purple swept-back star and yellow clustered anthers. Unlike S. triquetrum's more separately visible free yellow anthers, S. dulcamara anthers are tightly crowded. Rare WHITE-flowered S. dulcamara makes color alone insufficient.

items.label: 2 — RIPE red berries, DARK green calyces, individual stalks and lobed leaves
items.image_role: Ripe bright-red berries, dark five-lobed calyces, fruiting pedicels and basal-lobed leaves
items.creator: Piermario Maculan
items.caption: Ripe bright-red bittersweet nightshade berries at the end of their individual fruit stalks. Dark green/purplish five-lobed calyces are visible AT THE BASE of each ripe berry. The upper left leaf has small basal lobes. Photograph Piermario Maculan / GBIF occurrence 5938120478, CC0.
items.why_it_matters: Red berry color supports this red-fruited Solanum group but DOES NOT separate it from Texas nightshade. Observe calyx, berries, pedicels and leaves together.

items.label: LOOK-ALIKE — Texas nightshade (DIFFERENT SPECIES)
items.image_role: DIFFERENT SPECIES: Texas nightshade's usually WHITE corolla with yellow anthers visibly FREE and separate
items.creator: Joey Santore
items.caption: THIS IS TEXAS NIGHTSHADE (Solanum triquetrum), NOT BITTERSWEET. Note the usually WHITE, smaller flower with five more distinctly separate yellow anthers. White-flowered bittersweet exists, so compare leaf shape, angled stems, and cluster size as well. © Joey Santore, CC BY-NC 4.0; strictly noncommercial educational comparison only.
items.why_it_matters: Both plants can scramble and make red berries. S. dulcamara often has purple swept-back corolla, tightly clustered anthers, and MANY flowers (7–40) versus S. triquetrum's 3–6 and sharply triangular/hastate leaves.
